records.story: Bushmills prints 1608 on every bottle. As the house tells it, that is the year James I granted a local landowner a licence to distil in the district: a licence, not a distillery. The Old Bushmills Distillery Company was registered in 1784, and in 1885 a fire destroyed nearly all of the distillery, which was rebuilt. Prohibition in the United States closed the American market to Irish whiskey, Bushmills joined Irish Distillers in 1972, and by the late 1970s it was one of two whiskey distilleries at work on the island, beside Midleton in Cork. Pernod Ricard bought Irish Distillers in 1988, Diageo bought the distillery in 2005, and in 2014 Diageo agreed to hand Bushmills to Jose Cuervo in exchange for full ownership of Don Julio tequila. None of these changes altered the malt: it stayed triple distilled from malted barley alone. The soft, triple distilled Irish malt is measured by the 10 Year Old, the bottle to pour beside a peated Connemara.

records.story: Cooley Distillery's home at Riverstown, near Dundalk in County Louth, was a former state plant for industrial alcohol, which a group led by its founder took over in 1987. Converted to make whiskey, it began distilling in 1989, and it chose to distil its malt twice rather than three times. Connemara followed in 1996: a single malt made from barley dried over peat fires, reviving, as the house tells it, an old Irish habit in a whiskey better known for soft, unpeated malt. Cooley was sold to Beam in 2012, and Suntory bought Beam in 2014. Beside the bottling with no age statement, the house has released a 12 year old and a cask strength. Guests often ask whether Ireland makes smoky whiskey; this is the bottle that says yes, to taste beside a soft Bushmills or an Islay malt.

records.story: The name is older than the whiskey in the bottle. The Watt family ran a large distillery on Abbey Street in Derry, and the family's story is that in 1876 their horse The Tyrconnell won a race in Ireland at odds of a hundred to one, and that they named a whiskey for it to mark the win. The Watt distillery closed in the 1920s, and the name fell out of use. Cooley Distillery, founded in 1987 in a former state alcohol plant near Dundalk, brought it back as a single malt in the early 1990s; sources give the year as 1993 or 1994. Double distilled in pot stills and aged in bourbon casks, it became Cooley's plain malt, beside the peated Connemara that followed in 1996. Beam bought Cooley in 2012, and Suntory bought Beam two years later. The Tyrconnell carries two lessons to the bar: a revived Irish name need not come from its old distillery, and Cooley distils its malt twice where Bushmills distils three times.

records.story: Knappogue Castle is a tower house built in 1467 by the MacNamaras in the parish of Quin, County Clare. In 1966 a Houston businessman, a former Assistant Secretary of the United States Navy, bought it in ruins, and with his wife, an architect, he set about restoring it. Around the same time, by the brand's account, he began buying casks of pot still whiskey from Irish distilleries, aged them further and bottled them under the castle's name. In 1998 his son founded the company that became Castle Brands and brought the family's Knappogue Castle whiskey into it. Pernod Ricard agreed to buy Castle Brands in August 2019 and completed the purchase that October. The producer names no distillery, and accounts differ on whose stills made the malt over the years. An Irish single malt label and the distillery behind it can be two different things, and Knappogue Castle shows it: the castle on the label is a place to visit, not a distillery.

records.story: A husband and wife set up Walsh Whiskey in County Carlow in 1999, a company to blend and bottle an Irish Coffee, The Hot Irishman. By the house's account The Irishman was born in 2006, and Writers' Tears followed. Like many Irish labels of those years it was bottled from whiskey made at a distillery the house did not own. In 2016 the founders opened a distillery on the Royal Oak estate in Carlow with Illva Saronno, the Italian maker of Disaronno, as an equal partner. In January 2019 the two parted over how to grow the business: the distillery passed to Illva and was renamed Royal Oak Distillery, and the brands stayed with Walsh. Amber Beverage Group bought Walsh Whiskey in November 2021. Behind The Irishman Single Malt stands a house that buys and blends its whiskey, and the bottle shows that triple distillation and sherry wood are choices of style, not rules.
